title: Maleewa
author: Nabwile Joyce
desc: Smoked bamboo shoots from Mount Elgon soaked three hours in soda water, washed until the water runs clear, and simmered into groundnut paste — served to an honoured guest as a mark of respect.
longDesc: Maleewa is smoked bamboo shoots, cut young from the bamboo growing around Mount Elgon and then smoked and dried so they keep. It belongs to the Bagisu of eastern Uganda — Mbale, Sironko, Bududa, Manafwa, Bulambuli — and it is believed to help people live longer, which is why it is put in front of a special visitor and served at weddings. The alkali soak and the washing are the whole preparation: wash it until the water runs clear or the smoke turns bitter in the pot.
ingredients: 2 to 3 maleewa shoots, smoked and dried
5 ml (1 tsp) baking soda, or rock salt
equipment: Large bowl or pot, for the soak
steps: Put water in a large bowl or pot and stir in the baking soda or rock salt.
Submerge the dried smoked maleewa and leave it to soak for about 3 hours, or overnight.
Lift the maleewa out of the soda water. Wash it gently until the water is clear — this can take up to four washes. Drain.
Cut the soft parts away from the hard nodes, skipping the nodes, and slice the maleewa however you like.
Prepare your groundnut paste for cooking.
Once the groundnut stew starts to simmer, add the maleewa, curry powder, salt and black pepper, and stir well.
Let it simmer until it has reduced to a thick richness.
Take it off the heat and serve with your favourite starch.
chefTips: Wash it until the water runs clear. That removes the extra smokiness that would otherwise turn the dish bitter, and four washes is normal.
Do not throw the hard nodes away. Use them with other vegetables to make a stock — they give it a smoky flavour you cannot get any other way.
One shoot yields about a cup of chopped maleewa, so two or three feeds four.
Keep the seasoning light. Groundnut stew is sensitive, and curry powder, salt and pepper is all it wants.
Some cooks boil it in the soda water for 30 minutes instead of a three-hour cold soak. Both are documented and both work — the boil is faster, the soak is gentler.
Simsim paste instead of groundnut is equally traditional and gives a darker, nuttier result.

The step that makes maleewa maleewa — harvesting the young shoots, crushing, smoking and drying them — is not documented anywhere, so this recipe, like every other, starts from the dried smoked shoot as bought.
commonMistakes: Under-washing it, which leaves it bitter.
Skipping the alkali entirely, so it stays tough.
Cooking the hard nodes along with the soft parts.
Boiling the sauce hard once the paste is in, which splits it.
sources: Adapted from Sophia Musoki, 'How to Cook Maleewa (Smoked Bamboo Shoots)', A Kitchen In Uganda (2 August 2020) — all quantities, the soda soak, the wash-until-clear rule, the keep-the-nodes-for-stock tip and the one-shoot-to-one-cup yield are hers, as is the note on the longevity belief and its place at weddings.

The 30-minute alkali boil as an alternative to the cold soak is from Amor Desire, 'Bamboo Shoots (Malewa): A Delicacy of Eastern Uganda', Nexus Media (19 June 2023), which gives the method but no quantities.
Districts and the antiquity of the practice are from the Slow Food Foundation's Uganda booklet.
storage: Refrigerate up to 3 days. The dried shoots keep for months before soaking.
reheating: Warm gently with a splash of hot water.
healthBenefits: Bamboo shoots are high in fibre and low in calories, with potassium and some protein.
Groundnut paste brings protein and healthy fat.
Contains peanuts — not suitable for anyone with a nut allergy.
culturalNote: That maleewa is served to a special visitor as a sign of respect and love, because it is believed to lengthen life, tells you how it is understood — not as a vegetable but as something you give someone. The Bagisu have been eating it for a very long time, and the smoking that preserves it is what let a seasonal shoot become a year-round food.
